name: Ukraine
card_headline: Russia and Ukraine agreed a large prisoner swap in Abu Dhabi but no peace terms, as Russian strikes hit Kyiv's bridges and civilian deaths hit records
card_summary: Russia occupies about 20 percent of Ukraine and the front moved little this year. Talks in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November produced an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange and no deal on territory or security. Russian missiles and drones hit Kyiv's Dnipro bridges on 17 November, and the UN counted 372 civilians killed in October, 95 percent more than a year earlier. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi governs under martial law extended to 29 January 2027.
card_local: Kyiv Independent reports that Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov called a large prisoner exchange the main result in Abu Dhabi, with numbers undisclosed. [1] Ukrainska Pravda reports the UN count of 372 civilians killed in October. [2]
card_international: Reuters and Al Jazeera report online talks on 16 November with US envoys and Europeans while Kyiv's bridges and Russian refineries were struck. [3] AP's account of the opening day in Abu Dhabi notes that three earlier rounds in early 2026 produced no significant breakthroughs. [4]
card_scholar: ISW assesses that Russia's claimed recruitment results are likely inflated and that neither side advanced on 18 November. [5] Carnegie argues that Ukraine's manpower problem is mainly one of turning a large pool of citizens into trained soldiers. [6]
context_md: Russia launched its full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022, after seizing Crimea in 2014 and fighting in Donetsk and Luhansk from May 2014. [7] Martial law has applied since the first day of the invasion, and no national election has been held since. [8] Russia now occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukrainian territory, including all of Luhansk. [7] The United States paused aid in March 2025 and is now mainly a mediator, while the EU provides more total assistance than any other backer. [7] Ukraine became the 125th state party to the International Criminal Court in January 2026. [9] The IMF approved an $8.1 billion four-year programme in February 2026. [10]

sections.title: Abu Dhabi produced a prisoner swap agreement and no deal on territory or security
sections.body_md:
US-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations opened in Abu Dhabi on 10 November. Russia's chief negotiator was Vladimir Medinsky and Ukraine's delegation was led by Rustem Umerov, with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff involved. [4] It was the first round bringing US, Ukrainian and Russian officials together in nine months, and three earlier rounds in early 2026 had produced no significant breakthroughs. [3][4] The talks ended on 11 November with an agreement in principle on a large-scale prisoner exchange. [11] Neither side disclosed numbers. Zelensky had said the sides discussed a 1,000-for-1,000 or 1,500-for-1,500 format, and TASS cited a Russian general saying more than 1,000 on each side. [1] The latest completed swap, on 23 October, returned 270 people each way and was the 11th of 2026. [1]

Territory and security were not settled. Kushner said progress was made on a post-war security framework and that territorial issues would be the hardest to settle. [11] Medinsky said European security was a central topic and called the post-war security system "sick". [12] ISW reports that Kremlin aide Yuriy Ushakov restated Russia's 2021 demands to halt NATO expansion and return NATO to its 1997 configuration, and that Moscow would accept Europeans only in talks on a new European security architecture. [13]

On 16 November Ukraine held online talks with Witkoff, Kushner and European representatives and agreed to meet in Berlin with the Coalition of the Willing. [3] Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to widen the talks and that no date was set. [3] Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow wants a lasting peace and not a temporary ceasefire. [3] A three-day ceasefire agreed in May collapsed quickly. [7]

lenses.local: Kyiv Independent quotes Umerov saying the main result was agreement on a large-scale exchange, with the teams now working on details. [1]
lenses.international: AP and Reuters report no breakthrough in Abu Dhabi and Russian resistance to European participation in the three-way format. [4][3]
lenses.scholar: ISW reads Russia's proposed local ceasefire at Kostiantynivka as a likely bid to build up forces for a push toward Druzhkivka. [13]

sections.title: The front line barely moved in 2026, and Moscow's territorial claims run far ahead of it
sections.body_md:
ISW assessed that neither side advanced on 18 November. [5] Russian forces are attempting infiltration at Kostiantynivka, Kupiansk and near Slovyansk, and Ukrainian forces counterattacked southeast of Orikhiv and southeast of Kupiansk. [5] The long battle for Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad ended with Ukrainian forces pulling back to lines on the outskirts, according to Ukrinform's February review, which called the withdrawal a regrouping. [15] ISW's 18 November report mentions Pokrovsk as part of Russia's aim to encircle Ukraine's fortress belt in Donetsk from the southwest. [5]

Moscow's figures run far ahead of this. Putin said Russian forces took about 6,500 square kilometres and 310 settlements since the start of 2026. As reported by UNITED24 Media, ISW counts a net Russian gain of about 144.5 square kilometres from January to September and a net loss of about 122 square kilometres since 1 September. [14] That rests on one secondary report of ISW's figures. ACLED recorded about 200 settlements seized by Russia in 2025 and said the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration may decide Ukraine's fate in the region. [16] CFR puts Russian occupation at roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, with Ukraine holding about 19 percent of Donetsk. [7] ISW's own Donetsk estimate, relayed by UNITED24, is slightly higher at above 20 percent. [14]

Ukraine is also striking deeper. It hit the Kerch Strait Bridge on 16 and 17 November and the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries on 17 and 18 November. [5] CFR reports that Ukrainian drones sank a Russian corvette in Benghazi, Libya, on 23 November. [7]

lenses.local: Ukrinform's February review put Russian weekly gains at about 33 square kilometres in mid-February, down from 130 to 150 in mid-2025. [15]
lenses.international: Al Jazeera and Reuters report that Russia's defence ministry called Ukraine's 17 November attack the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia of the war. [3]
lenses.scholar: ISW says a Russian claim of a capture near Dobropillya is about 10 kilometres from the nearest assessed Russian infiltration area. [5]

sections.title: Civilian deaths are at record levels as Russia hits the power grid and Kyiv's bridges
sections.body_md:
The UN human rights office counted 372 civilians killed and 1,981 injured in Ukraine in October 2026, 95 percent more than in October 2025. Russian long-range drone and missile strikes caused 55 percent of the casualties. [5][2] September had been a record month with 328 killed and 2,105 wounded, up 85 percent on September 2025. [19] From January to September the UN counted 2,570 killed and 15,211 injured, 59 percent more than in the same period of 2025. [19] Kyiv recorded casualties on 22 of 30 days in September, more than in any month since the full-scale invasion began. [19]

On 17 November Russia launched ballistic and cruise missiles and 306 long-range drones, 92 of them jet-powered, according to the Air Force as reported by Kyiv Independent. The Northern and Southern bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv were damaged and closed, and water and heat supply were disrupted. Local authorities reported 14 killed and 78 injured across Ukraine that day. [17] Meduza reports that Russia began striking Kyiv's Dnipro bridges in October. [18]

Ukraine's Ministry of Energy counts more than 1,000 Russian strikes on energy infrastructure since early September, mostly on high-voltage substations. Strikes on sites where repairs were nearly done force crews to repeat work, hourly outage schedules run in most regions, and some regions have round-the-clock schedules. [20] About 700,000 households in Dnipropetrovsk lost power on 17 November. [17] HRW called 2025 the deadliest year for civilians since the full-scale invasion began. [9]

lenses.local: Ukrainska Pravda and LIGA.net carry the UN monthly counts, and the Energy Ministry's own update is the main source on outages. [2][19][20]
lenses.international: Reuters reports Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the two Dnipro bridges were reportedly hit and Reuters witnesses heard loud explosions. [3]
lenses.scholar: HRW attributes most 2025 civilian casualties in Kherson and Donetsk to Russian short-range drones that deliberately targeted civilians. [9]

sections.title: A $70 billion gap for 2027, ports under fire and an economy that has stopped growing
sections.body_md:
Ukraine's economy contracted in 2026. GDP fell 0.7 percent year on year in the third quarter, the central bank expects a 0.4 percent fall for the year, and inflation is expected to reach 12.5 percent. [21] The IMF's February programme had assumed real growth of 1.8 to 2.5 percent for 2026. [10] The IMF began a combined second and third review on 9 November that could unlock about $1.67 billion. [21]

Financing is the larger problem. The IMF put the four-year financing gap at $136.5 billion and the 2026 gap at $52 billion. [10] The EU's EUR 90 billion loan is meant to cover two thirds of external needs in 2026 and 2027, at EUR 45 billion a year, and Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko said in April that the 2026 gap was fully covered. [22] Ukrainian officials now say next year's funding gap is about $70 billion. [21] In April bne IntelliNews put the 2027 shortfall at about EUR 19 billion. [23] The two figures come from different sources and dates and are not reconciled here.

Exports are under pressure. The Black Sea corridor carries about 90 percent of Ukraine's agricultural exports, which earned $22 billion last year, and in July shipowners were halting calls at Ukrainian ports after Russian attacks. Between 20 June and 20 July Russia attacked 28 civilian vessels in Greater Odesa ports, killing 21 people, according to the Odesa Regional Prosecutor's Office. [24] The corridor has not been officially closed, though Reuters describes Black Sea exports as blocked. [24][21] Al Jazeera reports that a freighter sank off Bulgaria on 28 October with all 18 crew rescued, that Kyiv blames Russia, and that Ukrainian strikes on Russian cargo ships also intensified from July. Zelensky says Ukrainian forces did not operate in that area. [25] Analyst Aleksey Kushch says up to 60 million tonnes may be harvested but only about half can be shipped. [25]

lenses.local: Kyiv Independent quotes agribusiness club head Oleh Khomenko calling the corridor's situation a "de facto slowdown". [24]
lenses.international: Reuters reports that Russian air attacks have hit businesses, energy infrastructure and revenue-generating sectors. [21]
lenses.scholar: The IMF describes risks to its programme as exceptionally high and says it will be recalibrated if peace negotiations succeed. [10]

sections.title: Corruption cases have reached the president's former chief of staff, and martial law now runs to January 2027
sections.body_md:
Parliament voted on 26 October to extend martial law until 29 January 2027, with 293 votes, and extended general mobilisation with 281. [28] Ukraine has held no national election since the invasion because martial law bars them. Zelensky did not cancel elections, the Kyiv Independent wrote in 2025, and without martial law his term would have ended on 20 May 2024. [8]

Parliament approved Sergii Koretskyi, the former head of Naftogaz, as prime minister on 16 July as part of a government reshuffle. [26] Euronews reports NABU and SAPO investigations that reach into the president's circle. Operation Midas, unveiled in November 2025, alleges that a group influenced the state nuclear company Energoatom and laundered about EUR 85 million. Timur Mindich, a longtime friend and former business partner of Zelensky, is a suspect and left for Israel in November 2025. In May 2026 former chief of staff Andriy Yermak was named a suspect in a separate case, which he denies. In August Zelensky fired deputy chief of staff Iryna Mudra as NABU opened another probe. Zelensky has not been named a suspect in any of them. [27]

Ukraine opened the Fundamentals cluster of EU accession talks in June 2026, which covers the rule of law and anti-corruption. [27] HRW noted that an attempt in 2025 to weaken the two anti-corruption bodies drew criticism and was rolled back. [9]

lenses.local: Ukrainska Pravda reports the vote counts for the martial law extension, 293 and 281. [28]
lenses.international: Euronews reports the probes in detail and cites no public statement by Zelensky on them. [27]
lenses.scholar: HRW lists high-level corruption scandals and threats against anti-corruption activists and journalists among Ukraine's domestic rights concerns. [9]

sections.title: Ukraine's problem is turning a large pool into soldiers, and Russia's recruitment claims are disputed
sections.body_md:
Carnegie's March paper by Viktor Kevliuk, Olesya Favorska and Andriy Zagorodnyuk argues that Ukraine's manpower shortfall is mainly a problem of training and retention. After casualties, exemptions and emigration a substantial pool of military-age citizens remains. [6] The authors say some units recruit well under the same national framework and that personnel drift toward effective ones, which strains weaker units. [6] They attribute rising AWOL cases mainly to poor service conditions rather than reduced willingness to fight. [6]

On the Russian side, the Defense Ministry claimed on 17 November that it had met 89.3 percent of its 2026 recruitment plan, and ISW assesses the figure is likely inflated. [5] Ukraine's General Staff data, as cited by ISW, shows over 420,000 Russian casualties in 2026, with October the highest monthly loss rate of the war. [5] Meduza reports that nobody has been drafted under Russia's 2022 partial mobilisation since late that year, that analyst Janis Kluge estimated roughly 1,000 recruits a day in the second quarter, and that there is no reliable estimate of Russian military losses for 2026. [29] Levada Center data cited by Meduza shows support for continuing the war rising since early 2026, with a caveat that wartime polling deserves skepticism. [29]

lenses.international: Meduza, an exiled Russian outlet, says Putin ruled out a new mobilisation only for today and that Moscow has so far relied on contract recruitment. [29]
lenses.scholar: Carnegie's authors cite Ukrainian officials estimating that robotic integration could cut losses by roughly 30 percent. [6]

sections.title: 5.9 million Ukrainians are refugees, 3.7 million are displaced at home, and thousands of children were taken to Russia
sections.body_md:
UNHCR's year-end 2025 report counts about 5.9 million Ukrainian refugees abroad, over 5 million of them in Europe, and about 3.7 million internally displaced people, a total of about 10.3 million. Roughly 12.7 million people needed assistance, and UNHCR received 44 percent of the $803 million it required for the Ukraine situation. [30] HRW gives similar figures, with about 5.7 million refugees. [9]

The Yale School of Public Health's Humanitarian Research Lab reported on 25 March that Gazprom and Rosneft financed the transfer and ideological re-education of at least 2,158 children from occupied Donetsk, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia between 2022 and 2025, and it named six camps in Russia and Crimea. [31] This is Yale's finding as reported by Ukrainska Pravda. [31]

RSF counts 16 journalists killed by Russian forces since 2022 and 26 Ukrainian journalists jailed in Russia and occupied territories. It says 333 media outlets have closed, weakened by a collapsed advertising market and suspended USAID funding. [32] In occupied areas HRW reports that Russia coerces residents into taking Russian citizenship, conscripts Ukrainians, and holds thousands of POWs and detained civilians in inhumane conditions with systematic torture. [9]

lenses.local: Ukrainska Pravda's report on the Yale study says about 80 percent of the 44 entities and individuals involved are not under US or EU sanctions. [31]
lenses.international: UNHCR reports a funding gap of $453 million for the Ukraine situation at the end of 2025. [30]
lenses.scholar: Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab identified 44 legal entities and individuals involved in the transfers of children. [31]

timeline.text: Russia seizes Crimea after protests in Kyiv, and armed conflict begins in Donetsk and Luhansk in May.
Russia launches its full-scale invasion, and martial law is declared the same day.
The United States pauses aid to Ukraine.
Trump and Putin meet in Alaska without a deal.
NABU and SAPO unveil Operation Midas, alleging a kickback scheme around Energoatom.
Ukraine becomes the 125th state party to the International Criminal Court.
The IMF board approves an $8.1 billion four-year programme.
Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reports that Gazprom and Rosneft funded the transfer of at least 2,158 Ukrainian children.
A three-day ceasefire collapses, and former chief of staff Andriy Yermak is named a suspect in a corruption case.
Ukraine opens the Fundamentals cluster of EU accession talks.
Parliament approves Sergii Koretskyi as prime minister.
Parliament extends martial law to 29 January 2027.
US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks open in Abu Dhabi.
The Abu Dhabi talks end with an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange and no breakthrough on territory or security.
Russian missiles and drones damage Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges, and Ukraine strikes the Kerch Strait Bridge.
Ukraine strikes the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries as Putin attends the APEC summit in China.
A Russian drone enters Polish airspace during overnight strikes on Ukraine, the second such violation in a week.

factchecks.claim: Zelensky refused to hold elections and is no longer a legitimate president.
factchecks.by: Statements by Donald Trump and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov in February 2025
factchecks.evidence: The Kyiv Independent reports that Ukrainian law bars elections under martial law, which began on 24 February 2022, and that Zelensky did not cancel them. His term would have ended on 20 May 2024 without martial law. Parliament extended martial law again on 26 October 2026. The question of when a vote can be held is separate and is under discussion in talks.

factchecks.claim: Kostiantynivka can be handled with a local humanitarian ceasefire like the one in occupied Oleshky.
factchecks.evidence: ISW says the comparison is false because Russia does not control Kostiantynivka, where it has observed at least 41 Ukrainian positions since 1 September, and assesses Russia likely wants the pause to build up forces for a push toward Druzhkivka.

sources.title: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 13, 2026

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera cover the war and the talks daily, and ISW publishes a daily assessment [3][4][5]. Ukrainian outlets such as Kyiv Independent and Ukrainska Pravda file continuously, and the UN publishes monthly casualty counts [1][2][19]. What is thinner is reporting from occupied territory, where this draft relies on rights groups and a Yale study [9][31].

severity.basis: The UN counted 372 civilians killed in October 2026, 95 percent more than a year earlier, and Russia launched missiles and 306 long-range drones in a single day on 17 November [5][17].
UNHCR counts about 10.3 million refugees and internally displaced people and 12.7 million in need at the end of 2025, and strikes on the grid have brought hourly outages to most regions [30][20].

Martial law runs to 29 January 2027 with no national election since 2022, anti-corruption cases reach the former chief of staff, and in occupied areas Russia holds thousands of detainees while 26 Ukrainian journalists are jailed [28][27][9][32].
GDP fell 0.7 percent year on year in the third quarter, inflation is expected at 12.5 percent and officials cite a $70 billion funding gap for 2027 [21].
Civilian casualties rose 95 percent year on year in October, strikes on the grid exceed 1,000 since September and Kyiv's bridges are now targets, though the talks produced a swap deal [5][20][17][1].

parts.basis: The United States is mediating, Russia is a party, the EU is the largest donor, and Putin discussed the talks with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit [7][5].
Before 2022 about a third of world grain exports passed the Black Sea, and Ukraine supplied about 10 percent of global wheat exports and 15 percent of corn [25].
A Russian drone entered Polish airspace on 24 November for the second time in a week, and Finland summoned Russia's ambassador over an alleged helicopter violation [7].
About 5.9 million Ukrainian refugees are abroad, over 5 million of them in Europe [30].

Ukraine became the 125th state party to the ICC in January 2026, a Council of Europe damages register had over 70,000 claims by November 2025 and ISW reports six Western companies whose assets Russia seized donated to Russian military charities [9][13].

summary: Ukraine matters beyond its borders through great-power negotiation, Black Sea grain and energy flows, and spillover into Poland, Finland and Estonia [7][25].
gi.up: A Russian strike that kills people in a NATO member state, or a closure of the Black Sea corridor.
gi.down: A ceasefire with monitored lines and a funded 2027 budget.

gaps: Local Ukrainian-language sourcing is limited: Ukrainian outlets were read in English editions only, and the manpower section has no local lens because no Ukrainian source on mobilisation was read.
Russian independent outlets are represented by Meduza alone; Novaya Gazeta Europe and other exiled outlets were not opened. Russian state media appear once (TASS) and are flagged.
The Ukrainska Pravda article on the UN October casualty count failed to load; the figure is read from its search headline and matches ISW's report of the same UN data.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission's own reports were not opened; casualty counts come through Ukrainska Pravda, LIGA.net and ISW.
The ISW assessment of 16 October behind the territorial-gain figures could not be fetched; the figures come from one secondary report (UNITED24 Media).
Prisoner swap numbers were not disclosed as of the sources read, and implementation was not confirmed by 25 November.
Funding gap figures differ ($70 billion from officials via Reuters, EUR 19 billion from bne IntelliNews, IMF figures from February) and were not reconciled.
Sources conflict on the Black Sea corridor: Reuters describes exports as blocked, Kyiv Independent says the corridor is slowed but not closed.
The status of Pokrovsk and Myrnohrad rests on a February 2026 Ukrinform review; a current check was not made.
Occupied territories, Crimea, nuclear plant safety, war crimes accountability and Ukraine's own abuses (for example detention practices and mobilisation complaints) are covered thinly or not at all.
Reporter entries describe only the bylines read; the book entries were taken from publisher or institute pages and the Hachette and Harvard pages were not opened in full.
The Carnegie podcast page gives no episode length, and the year of 20 Days in Mariupol is inferred from the page's references to 2023.

local_md:
Kyiv Independent quotes Umerov saying the main result was agreement on a large-scale exchange, with the teams now working on details. [1]

Ukrinform's February review put Russian weekly gains at about 33 square kilometres in mid-February, down from 130 to 150 in mid-2025. [15]

Ukrainska Pravda and LIGA.net carry the UN monthly counts, and the Energy Ministry's own update is the main source on outages. [2][19][20]

Kyiv Independent quotes agribusiness club head Oleh Khomenko calling the corridor's situation a "de facto slowdown". [24]

Ukrainska Pravda reports the vote counts for the martial law extension, 293 and 281. [28]

Ukrainska Pravda's report on the Yale study says about 80 percent of the 44 entities and individuals involved are not under US or EU sanctions. [31]
international_md:
AP and Reuters report no breakthrough in Abu Dhabi and Russian resistance to European participation in the three-way format. [4][3]

Al Jazeera and Reuters report that Russia's defence ministry called Ukraine's 17 November attack the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia of the war. [3]

Reuters reports Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the two Dnipro bridges were reportedly hit and Reuters witnesses heard loud explosions. [3]

Reuters reports that Russian air attacks have hit businesses, energy infrastructure and revenue-generating sectors. [21]

Euronews reports the probes in detail and cites no public statement by Zelensky on them. [27]

Meduza, an exiled Russian outlet, says Putin ruled out a new mobilisation only for today and that Moscow has so far relied on contract recruitment. [29]

UNHCR reports a funding gap of $453 million for the Ukraine situation at the end of 2025. [30]
scholar_md:
ISW reads Russia's proposed local ceasefire at Kostiantynivka as a likely bid to build up forces for a push toward Druzhkivka. [13]

ISW says a Russian claim of a capture near Dobropillya is about 10 kilometres from the nearest assessed Russian infiltration area. [5]

HRW attributes most 2025 civilian casualties in Kherson and Donetsk to Russian short-range drones that deliberately targeted civilians. [9]

The IMF describes risks to its programme as exceptionally high and says it will be recalibrated if peace negotiations succeed. [10]

HRW lists high-level corruption scandals and threats against anti-corruption activists and journalists among Ukraine's domestic rights concerns. [9]

Carnegie's authors cite Ukrainian officials estimating that robotic integration could cut losses by roughly 30 percent. [6]

Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab identified 44 legal entities and individuals involved in the transfers of children. [31]
